q.t: On an electric cell, the metal cap is the…
q.e: A cell has two terminals: the metal cap is + and the flat metal disc is −.

q.t: Two or more cells joined together make a…
q.e: A battery is several cells joined + to −, so they push current the same way.

q.t: The thin wire inside an incandescent lamp that glows is called the…
q.e: Current heats the filament until it glows and gives light.

q.t: LED stands for…
q.e: LED = Light Emitting Diode. It has no filament.

q.t: Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
q.e: Metals let current pass. Plastic, rubber and wood are insulators.

q.t: Which of these is an insulator?
q.e: Glass does not let current through. The other three are metals, which conduct.

q.t: When a switch is ON, the circuit is…
q.e: ON means the switch closes the gap, so the path is complete and current flows.

q.t: A complete, unbroken path for electric current is called…
q.e: Current can only flow when it can go all the way round, from one terminal back to the other.

q.t: Is it safe to experiment with the electricity from wall sockets?
q.e: Mains electricity can kill. Experiments should use only cells and batteries.

q.t: In the cell symbol, the longer line stands for the…
q.e: Long line = +, short line = −.

q.t: A lamp's filament is broken. Will it glow when connected?
o: Only if the cell is reversed
q.e: A broken filament leaves a gap in the circuit. With no complete path, no current flows, so no glow. Such a lamp is called fused.

q.t: Which wire of an LED goes to the + terminal of the battery?
q.e: The longer leg of an LED is its + terminal, and must meet the + side of the battery.

q.t: An LED stays dark, but works when turned round. Why?
o: An LED lets current flow only one way
q.e: An LED conducts in one direction only. Reversed, it blocks the current; flipped the right way, it glows.

q.t: Does an incandescent lamp glow if you swap its connections?
o: Only if the switch is open
q.e: Current through a filament heats it whichever way it flows, so the bulb glows either way round.

q.t: Why are electric wires made of metal covered in plastic?
o: Metal carries current; plastic keeps it from reaching us
q.e: Metal is a conductor, so it does the job. Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps you safe from the current.

q.t: Pencil lead (graphite) in a conduction tester makes the bulb glow. So graphite is…
q.e: If the bulb glows, current passed through. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts.

q.t: Outside the cell, current is taken to flow from…
q.e: By convention, current outside the cell goes from + to −.

q.t: A switch placed anywhere in a circuit can turn the lamp off because…
o: It only works next to the lamp
q.e: A circuit is one loop. Opening it at any point breaks the whole loop, so current stops everywhere.

q.t: Why are circuit diagrams drawn with symbols?
o: Everyone can read the same symbols
q.e: Standard symbols mean anyone, anywhere, can read and build the circuit from the drawing.

q.t: In the LED symbol, the triangle points in the direction…
q.e: The triangle shows the one direction the LED lets current through. The two small arrows show light coming out.

q.t: A torch has two cells. One is put in the wrong way round. What happens?
q.e: The reversed cell pushes against the other, so they cancel out and the lamp doesn't glow.

q.t: A lamp doesn't glow. Cells are correct and connections tight. What should you check next?
q.e: If the cells and joints are fine, a fused (broken) filament is the likely gap in the circuit.

q.t: You touch the free ends of a conduction tester to a coin. The bulb glows. Then to an eraser — no glow. This shows…
o: The coin conducts; the eraser insulates
q.e: The glow means the path was completed through the coin. No glow means the eraser blocked current.

q.t: Why does a battery make a torch glow longer than a single cell?
q.e: More cells, joined correctly, store and supply more energy — longer and/or brighter light.

q.t: An electrician wears rubber gloves. Why?
q.e: Rubber does not let current pass, so it protects the electrician from shocks.

q.t: In a circuit with a cell, a switch and a bulb, the switch is open. Which is true?
o: Current flows only to the bulb
Current flows only in the cell
q.e: An open switch is a gap. Current needs a complete loop, so none flows anywhere.

q.t: Which object would NOT complete a circuit if placed in a gap?
q.e: Dry wood is an insulator. The others are metals, which conduct.

q.t: In a battery, how are cells joined?
o: + of one touches − of the next
q.e: Joining + to − lets every cell push current the same way, like everyone pushing a cart from one side.

q.t: An LED glows only one way. A bulb glows either way. Which can be used to find the + and − ends of an unknown battery?
q.e: Because the LED glows only when its long leg meets +, its glow tells you which end is +. The bulb glows either way, so it tells you nothing.

q.t: A circuit diagram shows two cells drawn side by side as long–short–long–short lines. This symbol means…
q.e: Each long–short pair is one cell; several cells in a row make a battery.

q.t: A circuit has a cell, two bulbs and a switch in one loop. One bulb fuses. What happens to the other bulb?
q.e: There is only one path. A fused bulb breaks the loop, so current stops through the other bulb too.

q.t: Why do we say current flows from + to − 'outside the cell'?
o: That is the path through the wires and lamp
Inside the cell there is no current
q.e: The rule describes the external path — through the wires, switch and lamp — from + back to −.

q.t: Your torch flickers when shaken. The likely cause is…
o: An LED pointing the right way
q.e: A loose joint makes and breaks the path as it moves, switching the current on and off.

q.t: A student builds a tester and touches the ends to a steel spoon, but the bulb doesn't glow. Which is the most likely reason?
o: The circuit has a fault, e.g. a fused bulb
q.e: Steel is a metal and conducts. If the bulb stays dark, something else in the tester — a fused bulb, a flat cell or a loose wire — is wrong.

q.t: Which is safer to handle while repairing a switch board?
o: A screwdriver with a plastic handle
A screwdriver with a metal handle
q.e: The plastic handle is an insulator, so current can't pass through it to your hand.

q.t: Why is wet skin more dangerous near electricity?
q.e: Ordinary water carries dissolved substances that let current pass, so wet skin conducts more easily.

q.t: A circuit diagram shows an LED with its triangle pointing away from the + terminal of the cell. Will it glow?
o: Only if the switch is open
Only if the cell is reversed and the switch is open
q.e: The triangle shows the direction current can flow. Current leaves the + terminal, so if the triangle points away from +, the LED is the right way round and glows.

q.t: Which is the best everyday example of a switch?
o: A light switch on the wall
q.e: A wall switch opens or closes the gap in the circuit, turning the light off or on.

q.t: A battery made of 3 cells is drawn in a diagram. How many long lines would you expect?
q.e: Each cell has one long line (+) and one short line (−). Three cells → three long lines.

q.t: Which statement is FALSE?
o: A switch can be anywhere in the loop
q.e: Graphite (pencil lead) is a non-metal but conducts, so 'every non-metal is an insulator' is false.
